card.title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Free fall is uniform acceleration $g$ with no air resistance: all bodies fall alike. With one consistent sign convention, the three equations of motion give every free-fall result — dropped bodies ($h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$), bodies thrown up ($h_{max} = u^2/2g$, $T = 2u/g$), and mixed cases.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Dropped from rest: $v = gt$, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
Thrown up (up positive): $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$
Maximum height: $h_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$ (at $v = 0$)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Universality of Free Fall:** All bodies fall with the same acceleration $g \approx 9.8 ext{ m/s}^2$ in vacuum (no air resistance). This is a consequence of the equivalence principle — inertial mass equals gravitational mass. The Apollo 15 hammer-feather drop on the Moon confirmed this.  ·  **Sign Convention Discipline:** Choose one positive direction (e.g., up = +) and use it consistently. For up-positive: $a = -g$, $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - rac{1}{2}gt^2$. The sign of $g$ goes into the equation ONCE — never mix conventions.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Take $g = 9.8$ m/s² unless the question says 10 — and say which you used.  ·  Note 2: For a body thrown up, do not put $t = T/2$ anywhere except the top; the position equation is valid for the whole flight.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1 (dropped): a mango falls from a 20 m tree — $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{4} = 2$ s; strikes at $v = \sqrt{2(10)(20)} = 20$ m/s.  ·  Example 2 (thrown up): a ball goes up at 15 m/s — top after 1.5 s, $h_{max} = 11.25$ m, back in hand after 3 s at 15 m/s (symmetry).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Heavier bodies fall faster.' ✅ In free fall ALL bodies have the same acceleration $g$; observed differences come from air resistance — demonstrated by the Apollo 15 hammer–feather drop on the Moon.  ·  ❌ 'At the top of the flight, acceleration is zero because the body stops.' ✅ $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward at ALL points of the flight. If $a$ were zero at the top, the body would stay there!

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Solve five thrown-up problems: $h_{max}$, $t_{up}$, $T$, and return speed, all from $u$ and $g$.  ·  Task 2: Prove ascent time = descent time twice — once by equations, once by the $v$–$t$ graph symmetry.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: 'Maximum height' ⇒ remember $u^2/2g$; 'time to top' ⇒ $u/g$; both come from $v = 0$ in the first and third equations.  ·  Trick 2: Total flight time of a return throw: $T = 2u/g$ — read the word 'returns' and write it instantly.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Prove that the time of ascent equals the time of descent for a body projected vertically upward (neglect air resistance).  ·  Q2. A stone dropped from a bridge strikes the water in 3 s. Find the bridge height and the striking velocity ($g = 10$).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: NEB loves the ascent = descent proof — quote $v = u - gt$ at top and bottom points and use symmetry.  ·  Exam Tip 2: In 'velocity on reaching ground' questions, prefer $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$; finding $t$ first wastes a step and invites rounding error.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Universality of free fall — $g$ is the same for all masses (Galileo).  ·  Concept 2: Sign-convention discipline — one axis, one consistent $g$ sign per problem.  ·  Concept 3: Top-of-flight state — $v = 0$, $a = g$: zero velocity is not zero acceleration.  ·  Concept 4: Up–down symmetry — equal times and speeds at equal heights.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Free fall acceleration $g$ is independent of mass, size and material.  ·  At every instant of the flight, $a = g$ downward — including the top ($v = 0$, $a \ne 0$).  ·  Up–down symmetry: equal speeds at equal heights, equal times up and down.  ·  Use ONE sign convention throughout a problem; put $g$'s sign in consistently.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and falcon feather on the Moon (1971): both hit the dust together — the most-watched verification that $g$ is mass-independent.  ·  Vacuum-tube 'Guinea and feather' demonstrations in classrooms reproduce the same result; air resistance, not gravity, distinguishes everyday falls.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. A ball is thrown upward and rises 45 m. Find its initial speed and total time of flight.  ·  Q4. Show that a body thrown up returns to the starting point with the same speed, using $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$.  ·  Q5. A coin is dropped from a lift moving up at constant velocity 6 m/s. Find its acceleration relative to (a) the lift, (b) the ground.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: Always sketch the motion (up, top, down) and mark $v = 0$ at the top — diagrams earn marks and prevent sign slips.  ·  Exam Tip 4: State 'neglecting air resistance' in theory answers — it defines the free-fall model.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3 (through a window): a ball dropped past a 2 m window takes 0.1 s — speed at window top $\approx \frac{2}{0.1} - \tfrac{1}{2}(10)(0.1) \approx 19.5$ m/s, hence fall height $\approx 19$ m.  ·  Example 4 (two balls): one dropped and one thrown down at 10 m/s from the same tower stay $10t$ apart — both gain speed at $g$; the throw only adds a constant offset.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: At the top of its flight, a ball thrown upward has: → B  ·  A body dropped from rest falls h in 2 s. In 4 s it falls: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version works free fall entirely through the equations of motion with sign conventions and the up-and-down symmetry argument — the pattern NEB numericals follow.  ·  **Definition:** a freely falling body moves under gravity ALONE — no air resistance, no push after release. All bodies fall with the same acceleration $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² (take 10 m/s² in numericals) independent of mass — Galileo's famous result.  ·  **Sign convention method:** choose upward positive. Then for a body projected up at $u$: $v = u - gt$, $h = ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$. The SAME equations with $u = 0$ describe a dropped body; with the throw downward, $u$ enters negative.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Odd-number/1:4:9 patterns for falls from rest — quick checks on fall distances.  ·  Times: $t_{up} = t_{down} = \dfrac{u}{g}$, total flight $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$  ·  $n$-th second fall distance: $s_n = \tfrac{g}{2}(2n - 1)$ — ratio $1:3:5:7\ldots$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Up-Down Symmetry (No Air Resistance):** Time up = time down = $u/g$. Velocity at equal heights going up and down are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction. At the top, $v=0$ but $a=g$ downward — zero velocity does NOT mean zero acceleration.  ·  'Dropped' = $u = 0$; 'thrown' = $u \ne 0$ — the equations differ by the $ut$ term.  ·  Air resistance is neglected in free fall; it is what produces terminal velocity in reality.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Using $g = -10$ m/s² AND taking $h$ positive upward in $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. ✅ Put the sign in ONCE: either $g$ negative with up positive, or down positive with $g$ positive — never both conventions mixed.  ·  ❌ 'A body thrown up takes longer to rise than to fall.' ✅ Without air resistance the times are EXACTLY equal ($u/g$ each way); with air resistance the fall takes LONGER, not the rise.  ·  ❌ 'Velocity on returning to the thrower is less than the launch speed.' ✅ Equal in magnitude (symmetry). Only air resistance or bounce changes it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Treating 'dropped' and 'thrown down' identically. ✅ Dropped means $u = 0$; thrown down means $u \ne 0$ downward — the equations differ by that initial term.  ·  Example 5 (lift): a lift falls freely — objects inside float relative to the cabin because both cabin and objects have $a = g$ (weightlessness in free fall).  ·  Note 3: Impact-speed questions: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ works even when $t$ is unknown — fastest route.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 4: Two-body fall problems: write $y_1(t)$ and $y_2(t)$ with one origin; separation is their difference — accelerations add no relative change if both are $g$.  ·  Note 1: Fix one positive direction per problem; the sign of $g$ follows from it (up positive ⇒ $a = -g$).  ·  Note 2: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ gives impact speed without needing time — quickest route for drop problems.
